extracted.intended_audience: OSHA-regulated employers, industry stakeholders, unions, state plan agencies, safety professionals, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of evaluative criteria, requirements, and feasibility findings from OSHA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings. Includes engineering and administrative control options, monitoring/trigger guidance, and comparisons to consensus standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fans and facilitated ventilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fan usage in industrial settings is prevalent; fans support convective and/or evaporative heat loss and can lower occupational heat strain at lower cost compared to air-conditioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fans can be personalized (directed toward specific workers), transported to remote workspaces, and used during work or at cooling areas; examples include fans incorporated into chairs and ducts to increase cooling air flow. OSHA requests comments on current use and application of fans in indoor and outdoor settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazards and limitations of fan use
rubrics_metrics.description: Although fan use can be effective at reducing heat stress, fans may introduce additional hazards in some workplaces due to the increase in air movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In indoor settings where air contamination is a concern, fans may interfere with existing ventilation and increase worker exposure to hazards; work site evaluation may be needed to ensure fans do not interfere with ventilation designed to control dust and other air contaminants. OSHA requests comments on work settings where fans are not feasible due to contamination concerns and on what controls employers use where fans are contraindicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraindication for fan use at very high temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Research has shown that under certain conditions (e.g., high temperatures), fan use can increase the hazard of heat strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA requests comments on indoor work settings that may experience temperatures above 102°F and seeks information on what controls employers implement when fan use is contraindicated or when temperatures exceed 102°F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporative coolers as an engineering control
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaporative coolers use a fan to pass air over a pad or ceramic surface saturated with water; evaporation reduces the air temperature and can lower air temperatures by as much as 20°F in warm dry climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They consume much less energy than air-conditioning and can be used in buildings with openings to the outside; however, they are not as effective at relative humidity above 60%. Portable evaporative coolers are commercially available and can cover large areas (examples: up to 6,500 sq ft; lower air temps by up to 33°F). OSHA cites a NIOSH HHE demonstrating feasibility of evaporative cooler use in a glass plant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor break area control options
rubrics_metrics.description: For break areas, the proposed rule allows employers to utilize available air-conditioning systems or a combination of air movement and humidity control to promote evaporative cooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The latter can be achieved with widely available fans and humidity control devices. OSHA provides employers multiple control options for compliance and allows them to tailor controls to individual workplaces. OSHA preliminarily determined these engineering controls indoors are technologically feasible for most operations most of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for outdoor break areas (shade or air-conditioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the proposed rule, OSHA is requiring employers to provide a break area with shade or air-conditioning for outdoor workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shade reduces exposure to solar radiation and overall heat load. Portable pop-up canopies, tents, or natural shade (trees) are commonly used. The proposed rule would not allow mobile equipment or machinery to be used to provide shade for rest breaks due to potential safety hazards and potential for equipment to release radiant heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and design of shade structures for outdoor workers
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide variety of portable pop-up canopies are commercially available that can be easily set up and moved around for mobile work sites; tents constructed from netted fabric open on two sides provide ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes demonstrations of shaded rest areas (canopies, tents, stools) in agricultural interventions and cites enforcement data showing high prevalence of shaded break areas among inspected employers. OSHA recognizes challenges for highly mobile crews but finds many mobile options feasible (portable canopies, umbrellas, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-conditioning options for outdoor workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to air-conditioning for outdoor work settings is primarily provided through the use of vehicles, trailers, and nearby buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence supports feasibility in various outdoor situations (e.g., air-conditioned vehicles used as cool-down areas). OSHA cites studies and commentors (City of Phoenix, IBEW) supporting portable AC units and vehicles/trailers as cooling methods and requests comments on additional ways employers have used AC for outdoor workers and obstacles encountered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile workplace control options
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for mobile work sites include portable canopies for shade and, where electricity is available, trailers with air-conditioning or air-conditioned vehicle cabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA found examples of employers agreeing to provide shade in contract negotiations and cites collective bargaining language requiring access to an area with shade for at least five minutes; OSHA preliminarily determined controls for mobile worksites are technologically feasible using commercially available products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary technological feasibility finding (indoor/outdoor/mobile)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA preliminarily determined that requirements for the use of engineering controls are technologically feasible for most operations most of the time for indoor, outdoor, and mobile work sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule is programmatic and offers several control options, allowing employers to determine controls best suited to their work environment. OSHA reviewed current practices and concluded readily available technology can meet requirements; seeks comments on assumptions and other control options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using mobile equipment as shade
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would not allow mobile equipment or machinery to be used to provide shade for rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: potential safety hazards from unintended or accidental start up and movement of the equipment and potential for equipment to release radiant heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in heat exposure monitoring methods (WBGT vs heat index)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed standard requires employers to monitor heat conditions but allows employers flexibility to determine workers' heat exposure using multiple options (WBGT, heat index, local forecasts) depending on setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For outdoor work areas, employers may track local heat index forecasts or measure heat index or WBGT. For indoor work areas, the proposed standard requires employers to identify hazardous heat exposure areas and develop a monitoring plan that includes measurement of heat index or WBGT. OSHA allows flexibility because WBGT can be technically challenging to measure and weather forecasts are readily available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special procedures for vapor-impermeable clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: For workplaces in which employees wear vapor-impermeable clothing, the employer's Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Program (HIIPP) must specify procedures to protect employees while wearing vapor-impermeable clothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is allowing multiple exposure-determination options but requires specific HIIPP procedures where clothing affects heat transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat trigger levels (initial and high triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed standard specifies an initial heat trigger of WBGT equal to the NIOSH REL or a heat index (unadjusted) of 80 °F, and a high heat trigger of WBGT equal to NIOSH REL or a heat index (unadjusted) of 90 °F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is not specifying a third 'extreme' trigger as some consensus standards do. OSHA believes the two proposed triggers are sensitive and appropriate screening thresholds protective for workers and achievable for employers, following SBAR Panel recommendations to keep triggers simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydration requirement (water provision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both ANSI/ASSP and OSHA proposed standard would require employees have access to suitably cool water free of charge, in close proximity to working areas, and of sufficient quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA does not require electrolyte replenishment beverages; it notes concerns about sugar content and that regular meals with adequate water are generally sufficient. OSHA requests comment on whether electrolyte supplements/solutions should be required in addition to water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest break requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's proposed standard requires employers to provide a rest break if needed to prevent overheating at or above the initial heat trigger, and requires a rest break of at least 15 minutes every two hours at or above the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANSI/ASSP recommended scheduled rest breaks at its moderate action level but did not require them; OSHA requires rest breaks because evidence shows rest, water, and shade reduce HRI risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical surveillance (OSHA decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: ANSI/ASSP recommends a medical surveillance program for all workers covered by the standard; OSHA proposed standard does not include a medical surveillance requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA found medical surveillance and CPR/AED certification requirements impractical or logistically difficult across the broad scope of covered employers and could add considerable costs. OSHA still requires monitoring and not leaving employees exhibiting heat illness signs unattended, offering on-site first aid and emergency medical services when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling personal protective equipment (PPE) policy
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed standard specifies engineering controls and administrative controls but does not require the use of cooling PPE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If employers choose to provide cooling PPE (e.g., cooling vests), the employer must ensure that the cooling properties of the PPE are maintained at all times during use because cooling PPE can become hazardous as properties dissipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping requirement for indoor measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed standard requires that employers maintain written or electronic records of indoor work area measurements for 6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is more specific than ANSI/ASSP, which required a written inventory only as long as the hazard existed or as required by law; OSHA believes specificity increases clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of heat safety coordinator(s) vs qualified person
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed standard does not require a 'qualified person' as in ANSI/ASSP; instead the proposed standard requires designation of one or more heat safety coordinators trained in and responsible for ensuring compliance with all requirements of the employer's HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA believes requiring a qualified person would be infeasible across the widespread scope of the rule; OSHA will provide compliance assistance materials (model HIIPP, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard alert provision (notification of high heat trigger)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed standard contains a hazard alert provision that requires employers to notify employees that the high heat trigger has been met or exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is not present in the ANSI/ASSP standard and is a specific OSHA addition to ensure employees are made aware when high-heat conditions are reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for stakeholder comment on feasibility and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA requests comments on multiple technical and feasibility questions related to monitoring and controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific topics requested: feasibility of measuring HI in indoor environments; use of WBGT and situations where it is impractical; other controls or technologies; feasibility of dehumidification; areas where isolation of heat-producing equipment is not feasible and alternatives used; current use of air-conditioning; additional ways AC is used for outdoor workers; current use and application of fans; work settings where fans are infeasible due to contamination concerns; indoor settings without heat-generating processes that may experience >102°F and what controls are used when fans are contraindicated or when temperatures exceed 102°F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of consensus standards and justification for differences
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must consider adopting existing national consensus standards and, when differing substantially, publish reasons why its rule better effectuates the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA compared its proposed standard to ANSI/ASSP A10.50-2024 across scope, measurements, trigger levels, hydration, rest breaks, medical surveillance, PPE, recordkeeping, and qualified person requirements, noting where OSHA's approach differs and why (e.g., broader scope, more flexibility, cost/practicality concerns).
